newsitem.title: USA: U.S. factory orders, shipments up in April.
newsitem.headline: U.S. factory orders, shipments up in April.

text.p: U.S. factories were humming in April as new orders flowed in briskly and shipments of finished products picked up, the Commerce Department said Wednesday.

New orders rose a stronger-than-expected 1.2 percent to a seasonally adjusted $323.9 billion, rebounding from a 1.3 percent decline in March. It was the third increase in orders during the past four months and exceeded Wall Street economists' forcasts of a smaller 0.8 percent pickup in April orders.
Shipments also increased by 1.2 percent in April, to $325.6 billion, a fourth consecutive monthly rise following an 0.1 percent March gain.

Department officials said it was the strongest monthly pickup in shipments in a year, since a 2.4 percent increase in April 1996, reflecting the busy pace at factories at the start of the second quarter.

Consumer demand was exceptionally strong in the first quarter this year, when the economy was expanding at a booming 5.8 percent annual rate, so some businesses may have been replenishing their drawn-down inventories.

Commerce said order backlogs at factories decreased by 0.3 percent in both March and April -- the first back-to-back monthly drops in unfilled orders since July and August 1995, department officials said.
During April, orders for costly durable goods like new cars and refrigerators rose a revised 1.3 percent to $175.5 billion afrter a 2.2 percent drop in March.
Previously, on May 28, the department said April durable orders had risen 1.4 percent but it revised that down slightly.
Orders for nondurables like food and paper products increased 1 percent during April to $148.4 billion after a 0.3 percent decline in March.
The April factory orders report showed orders for transportation equipment rose 3.4 percent to $39 billion following a 3.9 percent decrease in March.

Shipments of motor vehicles and parts climbed 3.4 percent to $28.1 billion during April, more than recovering a 1.7 percent decline in March. In the automobile industry, shipments correspond to orders.
Excluding transportation, factory orders were up 0.9 percent in April after dropping 1 percent in March.
Manufacturing seems likely to remain brisk for some time to fill current orders. But weaker order backlogs over the past two months point to some easing in the pace of activity later in the year.
On Monday, the National Association of Manufacturers said its index of industrial activity picked up briskly and unexpectedly in May, in large part because new orders continued to grow strongly.
Defence contractors' orders, which are subject to wide monthly swings, shot up by 27.8 percent to $6.2 billion after a 12.2 percent drop March.
Orders for non-defence capital goods, a measure of business' expansion plans, fell 2 percent to $44.6 billion in April after a 3 percent plunge in March.
